**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw my name in print, it was in a police report. Not my own—someone else’s. A woman’s. Her name was *Lena Voss*, and the report listed her as *missing*. The date was three days ago. The officer who handed it to me had been drinking coffee that smelled like burnt sugar and regret. He didn’t look up when he said, *"You’re her next of kin."*

I didn’t know what to do with that. A name is just a name until it’s tied to a body. Until it’s tied to *you*.

---

**The Art of Disappearing**

I learned how to vanish at twelve. It wasn’t hard. Just stop moving. Stop talking. Stop *existing*. The world would forget you faster than you could say *"I’m sorry."* My mother taught me. She disappeared every time my father raised his hand. I watched her melt into the wallpaper, into the silence between breaths. I didn’t want to be like her—too passive, too quiet—but I wanted to be *safe*.

Now, at twenty-seven, I’ve perfected it. I’m the ghost in the corner of the room, the one who doesn’t take up space. The one who doesn’t ask for anything.

Except sometimes, when the lights flicker and the air smells like rain, I wonder what it would feel like to *not* disappear.

---

**The Last Letter**

I found it tucked inside an old book on the shelf of my grandmother’s attic. The paper was yellowed, the ink smudged at the edges like tears. It was addressed to her.

*My dearest Clara,*

*If you’re reading this, I’m already gone. The train leaves at dawn, and I won’t be able to write again. But I had to tell you—your silence is louder than any scream. I love you, even when you won’t look at me.*

*Your husband,*
*Daniel*

I traced the words with my fingers. My grandmother never spoke of him. Never mentioned the war, the letters, the things left unsaid. She just… stopped. Like a record skipping, then playing the same note over and over.

I wonder if she ever opened the window at night, just to listen for the sound of his voice.

---

**The Thing About Ghosts**

They say ghosts are just echoes. Fragments of people who didn’t get to finish their stories. My great-grandmother was one of them. She died before I was born, but I’ve seen her in the photographs—her dark eyes, her sharp chin, the way she held her head like it was made of glass.

I tell people she was a poet. That she wrote love letters in the margins of her Bible. That she dreamed of a life beyond the farm, beyond the dust, beyond the men who told her what to do.

It’s not true. But it’s the closest I’ve ever come to knowing her.

---

**The Weight of a Name (Again)**

Now, my name is on a birth certificate. A little girl’s. Her name is *Elena*. She has my eyes, my mother’s silence, and my father’s stubbornness. She doesn’t know yet that names are just labels. That they can be taken. That they can be *given away*.

I hold her hand as we walk past the old police station. The one where my name was first written down. The one where I learned that some things—like love, like fear, like the weight of a name—are heavier than you think.

Elena squeezes my fingers. *"Mama,"* she says, *"why do you cry?"*

I don’t answer. I just pull her closer.

Some things don’t need words.
